title: Decompose dashboard aggregator into streaming handlers and per-route LRU cache
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Background: The console backend currently uses a monolithic dashboard aggregation handler that fan-outs to multiple GraphQL resolvers and internal REST endpoints synchronously. This pattern has produced unpredictable tail latency and high CPU/memory churn under burst load, contributing to several customer-facing UI slowdowns. Previous work (ENG-6123, ENG-8231) addressed cache invalidation semantics and some GraphQL query shaping but left the central aggregator and route-level caching unaddressed.

Objective: Reduce P95/P99 console page load latency and CPU variance by decomposing the aggregator into streaming/async handlers, implementing a bounded per-route in-memory LRU cache with explicit memory budget and eviction instrumentation, and tightening resolver timeouts and backpressure. The change should be transparent to frontend routes and support gradual rollout.

Proposed work:
- Introduce a streaming handler abstraction (Node service) that returns partial payloads as sub-responses arrive, reducing blocking for long-running internal requests.
- Replace single-threaded monolith aggregator with a coordinator that issues parallel requests and merges results incrementally.
- Add per-route LRU caches with configurable TTL and size (route metadata: cacheable=true|false, max_entries). Use an off-heap map (node-cache backed by shared memory) where possible to reduce GC pressure.
- Expose cache metrics: hit/miss, evictions, average entry size, and memory footprint per-route.
- Add end-to-end tracing/span tags for aggregator->resolver RPCs and cache hits to attribute latency sources.
- Update GraphQL resolvers to return streamable fragments (schema-compatible) and add safe timeouts/fallback payloads for missing fragments.
- Automated canary: enable streaming+cache for 5% of traffic, monitor latency and error rates for 48h, then 25%/75%/100% rollouts.

Acceptance criteria:
- Console home/dashboard P95 latency reduced by >=20% in canary compared to baseline.
- P99 tail improved and CPU variance during simulated bursts reduced by >=15%.
- Cache hit rate >= 40% for targeted routes after 2 days of traffic.
- No increase in 5xx rate above baseline (allowed +0.1%).
- Observability: dashboards for cache metrics, per-route latency breakdown, and flamegraphs for aggregator.

Risks and mitigations:
- Memory pressure from caching: enforce strict per-route budgets and eviction policies; add circuit-breaker to disable caching if node memory crosses threshold.
- Serialization incompatibilities with frontend: maintain identical JSON schema and run integration tests.
- Increased deployment complexity: ship behind a feature flag and use progressive rollout automation.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for streaming handler behavior and cache eviction logic.
- Integration tests emulating slow downstream resolvers and asserting partial responses are forwarded.
- Load test with synthetic traffic mixes (bursty and steady) to validate CPU/latency improvements.
- Canary verification and automated rollback hooks.

Rollout plan:
1) Feature branch with feature-flagged streaming + in-memory LRU cache.
2) Internal staging smoke tests + perf benchmark.
3) Canary 5% for 48h, monitor; expand to 25% then 75% if metrics meet thresholds.
4) Full rollout and post-mortem within 2 weeks.

Notes: This ticket intentionally differs from prior aggregator work by focusing on streaming partial responses and placing bounded caches at the route boundary rather than global cache layers. Coordination with infra (memory accounting) and observability (new metrics) is required.
